Optical fibers are used in both classical telecommunications and quantum communication and could serve not only as connections between computing nodes but also as quantum processors themselves in the future. The results, published in Nature Physics, pave the way for new technologies in quantum signal processing.

Science.title: About 2% of natural gas supplied to a Midwest city leaks into the atmosphere
Science.summary: Most natural gas leakage in Indianapolis likely originates from homes and other buildings, not exterior pipelines and large-scale distribution infrastructure that deliver the fossil fuel, according to Penn State researchers who assessed nearly a decade of data.

Science.title: Sunlight gives biodiesel byproduct a second life as hydrogen and valuable chemicals
Science.summary: Australian researchers and international collaborators have demonstrated a solar-driven approach to convert glycerol, a low-value byproduct of biodiesel production, into hydrogen and higher-value chemicals. Using advanced techniques at the Australian Synchrotron, they revealed how the catalyst changed while it was working.

Science.title: Antarctica’s sea ice has undergone a stunning reversal
Science.summary: Antarctic sea ice reached its third-lowest winter maximum in 2026, extending a remarkable decline that began after years of record-breaking growth. Scientists are investigating whether the dramatic reversal signals a long-term shift in Antarctica's frozen landscape.

Science.title: 'Dark Matter's' Joel Edgerton and Jennifer Connelly talk S2's marital disintegration and the humility of hanging on wires (interview)
Science.summary: 'It makes you think about how you can be a better person in life. And there’s always room for improvement.'

Science.title: Scientists discover a plastic-eating “Pac-Man” enzyme with a surprising secret
Science.summary: Scientists have discovered a remarkable “Pac-Man enzyme” that helps bacteria devour certain types of plastic and may offer new hope in the fight against plastic pollution. Researchers found that several biodegradable plastics completely broke down in soil within about a year, while conventional plastic remained largely unchanged.

Science.title: Physicists froze a 'necklace' of atoms — and witnessed a quantum phenomenon predicted 100 years ago
Science.summary: Atoms confined to a single line can bind into clusters called Bethe strings. A new experiment points to a mix of many such clusters, though the evidence is still indirect.

Science.title: Rocket Lab pushes 1st launch of next-gen Neutron rocket to 2027
Science.summary: Rocket Lab has delayed the debut of its powerful, partially reusable Neutron launcher to 2027 due to a manufacturing issue.

Science.title: What makes a place ready for radical innovation? Researchers say resident openness matters
Science.summary: Why do some cities embrace new technologies and business models while others are slower to take them up? Economic conditions, infrastructure and access to technology clearly matter. But a new study from the University of Amsterdam and the University of St Gallen suggests there is another factor that has received much less attention: the psychological openness of the local population. Regions where people are more open to new experiences and unfamiliar ideas are more likely to be early adopters of radical innovations, the study says.

Science.title: It's time to reassess the size of our solar system, scientists say
Science.summary: Two leading space scientists say there is a need to redefine the edge of the solar system based on the Milky Way's gravity, including its dark matter.

Science.title: A protein that fuels cancer could also be the key to fighting it
Science.summary: Scientists have discovered how to turn a protein that normally fuels cancer growth into a weapon against it. By activating PPARD in immune cells, researchers made them better at burning fat and attacking tumors, slowing or stopping cancer growth in laboratory experiments. The approach showed promise against colorectal, breast, and ovarian cancers, as well as melanoma.

Science.title: Unprecedented atlas explores mitochondria across the tree of life
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 16 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03195-9 The mitoproteomes of five parasites and a plant hold medical potential — and reignite the question of just when the mitochondrion evolved.

Science.title: Glowing liquids could help protect products from counterfeiters using distinctive ultraviolet light signatures
Science.summary: Researchers at Nottingham Trent University have developed room-temperature liquids containing chemical elements that produce distinctive patterns of light. They say the materials could provide a flexible new approach to optical tagging and anti-counterfeiting, while being compatible with existing processing and printing technologies.

Science.title: World-record intensity in attosecond hard-X-ray pulses could unlock closer study of electrons in atoms and molecules
Science.summary: Researchers used the European XFEL to create X-ray flashes that were not only extremely short but also reached record intensity for this type of pulse. The researchers focused the X-rays to an area roughly 100,000 times smaller than the cross section of a typical human hair. This concentrated the X-ray light into a tiny but extremely powerful spot. The method could enable detailed studies of how electrons behave in atoms and molecules and, in the long term, could even allow researchers to control electrons during chemical reactions. Science.title: The pianist who never played
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 16 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03112-0 A note to self.

Science.title: Adaptive molecular convergence more common than previously thought, distant jellyfish relatives reveal
Science.summary: A new study has found that adaptive molecular convergence—the process by which distantly related or unrelated species evolve the same genomic changes—is not as rare as previously thought.

Science.title: Beyond pointing your phone at the night sky, this is how to use stargazing apps effectively
Science.summary: There is no shortage of stargazing apps, but unless you use these tips, you may be missing out. Here are the best ways to get the most out of them.

Science.title: Briefing Chat: An invisible tattoo that appears under UV light – and then disappears
Science.summary: Nature, Published online: 16 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03341-3 Nature staff discuss a new ink that could be useful for medical tattooing — plus, an insight into why small dogs live longer than big ones.

Science.title: New alloy design strategy combines strength and ductility by timing hardening mechanisms
Science.summary: Structural metals used in engineering projects are expected to have both high strength and high ductility: the ability to withstand heavy loads and deform before failure. Achieving both of these properties at the same time, however, is challenging.

Science.title: A quantum highway just one atom high could transform superconductors
Science.summary: Scientists discovered that atomic steps just one atom high can guide quantum vortices through superconductors, making them move more than 1,000 times more easily in one direction than another. This remarkable control over quantum motion could lead to a new generation of ultra-efficient superconducting electronics.

Science.title: When not to watch a meteor shower — why I'm not staying up for the Orionids
Science.summary: The Orionid meteor shower peaks next week, but a bright moon makes much of the night less than ideal. Sometimes the sensible observing decision is knowing when to stay in bed — and when to get up early.

Science.title: Rabbits were a medieval royal luxury in England—until the Black Death made them commonplace
Science.summary: The European rabbit is a common sight in the British countryside today. Yet it was not always so. They are not native to the British Isles and are one of the most devastating invasive species.

Science.title: How to see the Orionid meteor shower 2026 peak this week — and when to look
Science.summary: The Orionids peak around Oct. 21. Here's when and where to look for the best chance of spotting meteors.
